focus: Exodus 18 brings Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, to the camp at the mountain of God, where he hears what the LORD has done for Israel, confesses that the LORD is greater than all the gods, and worships with Israel’s leaders. The next day he sees Moses judging the people alone from morning until evening and counsels him to share the work with able, God-fearing men, completing the journey from the sea to Sinai.

sections.title: Jethro Brings Moses’ Wife and Sons to the Mountain of God
sections.summary: Jethro hears all that God has done for Moses and Israel and comes to the wilderness with Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, whose names recall Moses’ exile and God’s help. He sends word that he is coming to Moses where he is encamped at the mountain of God.

sections.title: Jethro Blesses the LORD and Worships with Israel’s Leaders
sections.summary: Moses tells Jethro all that the LORD has done to Pharaoh and how He delivered Israel through every hardship, and Jethro rejoices and says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods” (Exodus 18:11). Jethro offers a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron and the elders eat bread with him before God.

sections.title: Jethro Counsels Moses to Share the Work of Judging
sections.summary: Seeing the people stand before Moses from morning until evening, Jethro warns, “The thing that you do is not good” (Exodus 18:17), because the burden will wear out both Moses and the people. He advises Moses to stand before God for the people and teach them God’s ways, and to appoint able men who fear God, men of truth who hate covetousness, to judge the ordinary cases, if God so commands.

sections.title: Moses Appoints Judges and Jethro Returns Home
sections.summary: Moses heeds his father-in-law, chooses able men out of all Israel, and makes them rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They judge the small cases and bring the hard ones to Moses, and Jethro departs to his own land.

1.brief: Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, hears all that God has done for Moses and Israel and how the LORD brought them out of Egypt. News of God’s deliverance reaches beyond Israel.
1.explain:
“And Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law,”

“Jethro” is introduced again as “the priest of Midian” and Moses’ father-in-law. Moses lived with him for forty years after fleeing Egypt (2:15–22; 3:1). In 2:18 he is called Reuel.

“heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel His people—that the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.”

Jethro “heard” what God had done. The news of the exodus has spread beyond Israel, as God intended (9:16; 15:14). News of God’s deliverance reaches beyond Israel.
1.notes: Jethro is also called Reuel (2:18) and possibly Hobab (Numbers 10:29; Judges 4:11). Interpreters differ on whether these are different names for the same man or whether Hobab was his son.

2.brief: Jethro takes Zipporah, Moses’ wife, whom Moses had sent back. Moses’ family is about to be reunited with him.
2.explain:
“Then Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her back,”

Jethro brings “Zipporah, Moses’ wife.” Moses had “sent her back” to her father at some point after leaving Midian. The text does not say when or why.
2.notes: Zipporah set out with Moses toward Egypt (4:20, 24–26). Some think Moses sent her home after the incident at the lodging place in 4:24–26. The text does not say.

3.brief: Jethro also brings her two sons, one named Gershom, because Moses said, “I have been a stranger in a foreign land.” The name recalls Moses’ years of exile.
3.explain:
“with her two sons, of whom the name of one was Gershom”

Jethro brings Moses’ “two sons.” The first is “Gershom” (2:22).

“(for he said, ‘I have been a stranger in a foreign land’)”

The name sounds like the Hebrew words for a stranger there. Moses named him to mark his years as an exile in Midian. The name recalls Moses’ years of exile.

4.brief: The other son is named Eliezer, because Moses said, “The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” The name testifies to God’s help in Moses’ life.
4.explain:
“and the name of the other was Eliezer”

The second son is “Eliezer.” His name has not appeared before in Exodus.

“(for he said, ‘The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh’);”

“Eliezer” means my God is help. Moses named him in thanks to the God who “delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh,” when Pharaoh sought to kill him (2:15). The name testifies to God’s help in Moses’ life.
4.notes: Gershom and Eliezer are listed among the Levites, not among the priests (1 Chronicles 23:14–17).

5.brief: Jethro comes with Moses’ sons and wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he is camped at the mountain of God. The meeting takes place where God first called Moses.
5.explain:
“and Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness,”

Jethro brings the family to Moses in the wilderness.

“where he was encamped at the mountain of God.”

Moses is camped “at the mountain of God,” Horeb or Sinai. God had told Moses at the burning bush, “you shall serve God on this mountain” (3:12). The meeting takes place where God first called Moses.
5.notes: Exodus 19:1–2 describes Israel arriving at Sinai. The narrative places Jethro’s visit and counsel here, at the mountain of God, before the account of the arrival and the giving of the law.

6.brief: Jethro sends word to Moses that he is coming with Moses’ wife and her two sons. The visit is announced and welcomed.
6.explain:
“Now he had said to Moses, ‘I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her.”

Jethro sends word ahead that he is coming. The visit is announced and welcomed.

7.brief: Moses goes out to meet his father-in-law, bows down and kisses him, and they ask each other about their well-being before going into the tent. The scene is one of honor and warm family reunion.
7.explain:
“So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down, and kissed him.”

Moses honors Jethro. He goes “out to meet” him, “bowed down,” and “kissed him.” These were customary signs of respect and affection.

“And they asked each other about their well-being, and they went into the tent.”

They greet each other with care. The Hebrew reads literally that they asked each other about peace. Then they go “into the tent” to talk. The scene is one of honor and warm family reunion.

8.brief: Moses tells Jethro all that the LORD did to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel’s sake, all the hardship on the way, and how the LORD delivered them. Moses gives God the credit for every part of the story.
8.explain:
“And Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel’s sake,”

Moses tells the whole story. He describes “all that the LORD had done” to Pharaoh and Egypt. The story is about what God did.

“all the hardship that had come upon them on the way, and how the LORD had delivered them.”

Moses does not hide “the hardship” of the journey, the thirst, hunger, and battle. But each hardship ends with “how the LORD had delivered them.” Moses gives God the credit for every part of the story.

9.brief: Jethro rejoices over all the good the LORD has done for Israel in delivering them from the Egyptians. He shares in Israel’s joy at God’s goodness.
9.explain:
“Then Jethro rejoiced for all the good which the LORD had done for Israel,”

Jethro “rejoiced” at God’s goodness to Israel. He shares in Israel’s joy at God’s goodness.

“whom He had delivered out of the hand of the Egyptians.”

Jethro rejoices specifically over the deliverance from Egypt.

10.brief: Jethro says, “Blessed be the LORD,” who delivered Israel from the Egyptians and from Pharaoh. A priest of Midian praises Israel’s God by name.
10.explain:
“And Jethro said, ‘Blessed be the LORD,”

A priest of Midian says “Blessed be the LORD.” He praises Israel’s God by His covenant name.

“who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh,”

Jethro names what God did. He delivered Moses and Israel from “the hand of the Egyptians” and “the hand of Pharaoh.”

“and who has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.”

Three times in the verse Jethro speaks of God’s deliverance from the “hand” of Egypt. He praises the God who broke Egypt’s grip on His people.

11.brief: Jethro confesses, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods,” because He was above them in the very thing in which they acted proudly. Hearing what the LORD has done brings Jethro to acknowledge His supremacy.
11.explain:
“Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods;”

Jethro makes a confession: “Now I know.” Hearing what the LORD has done brings him to acknowledge that “the LORD is greater than all the gods.” The plagues were meant to teach Egypt to know the LORD (7:5). They have taught a Midianite priest as well.

“for in the very thing in which they behaved proudly, He was above them.”

The second half of the verse is difficult in Hebrew. It means that where Egypt and its gods acted arrogantly against Israel, the LORD showed Himself superior. Many see an example in the sea: Egypt had tried to drown Israel’s sons in the Nile (1:22), and Egypt’s army was drowned in the sea.
11.notes: Interpreters differ on how far Jethro’s faith went. His words and actions should be the measure. He blesses the LORD, confesses Him greater than all gods, offers sacrifice, and eats before God with Israel’s leaders. Naaman later made a similar confession (2 Kings 5:15), as did Rahab (Joshua 2:11).

12.brief: Jethro offers a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron and the elders come to eat bread with him before God. Jethro’s confession leads to worship and fellowship with Israel’s leaders.
12.explain:
“Then Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took a burnt offering and other sacrifices to offer to God.”

Jethro brings “a burnt offering and other sacrifices.” His confession leads to worship.

“And Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God.”

Aaron and “all the elders” share a meal with Jethro “before God.” Eating together in God’s presence was a sign of fellowship and peace. Jethro’s confession leads to worship and fellowship with Israel’s leaders.

13.brief: The next day Moses sits to judge the people, who stand before him from morning until evening. The scene turns from worship to the daily work of leading Israel.
13.explain:
“And so it was, on the next day, that Moses sat to judge the people;”

The scene turns from worship to daily work. Moses sits “to judge the people,” hearing their disputes and questions.

“and the people stood before Moses from morning until evening.”

The people stand in line “from morning until evening.” The work never ends.

14.brief: Jethro asks, “What is this thing that you are doing for the people?” and why Moses sits alone while all the people stand around him all day. Jethro sees a problem Moses has not addressed.
14.explain:
“So when Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did for the people,”

Jethro watches Moses at work all day. He sees what Moses cannot see from inside the work.

“he said, ‘What is this thing that you are doing for the people?”

Jethro asks a probing question.

“Why do you alone sit, and all the people stand before you from morning until evening?”

He points to the problem. Moses sits “alone,” and the people wait all day. Jethro sees a problem Moses has not addressed.

15.brief: Moses answers that the people come to him to inquire of God. He explains his work as helping the people seek God’s direction.
15.explain:
“And Moses said to his father-in-law, ‘Because the people come to me to inquire of God.”

Moses explains his work. The people come “to inquire of God,” to seek God’s direction through Moses. He sees his role as helping the people seek God’s direction.

16.brief: Moses says that when they have a dispute he judges between them and makes known God’s statutes and laws. His work involves both settling disputes and teaching God’s ways.
16.explain:
“When they have a difficulty, they come to me, and I judge between one and another;”

When there is “a difficulty,” a dispute between people, Moses decides the case.

“and I make known the statutes of God and His laws.”

Moses also teaches “the statutes of God and His laws.” His work involves both settling disputes and teaching God’s ways.
16.notes: The statutes and laws Moses teaches here include God’s instruction given before Sinai, such as the commands at Marah (15:25–26) and about the Sabbath (16:23–29).

17.brief: Jethro tells him, “The thing that you do is not good.” The wise counsel begins with an honest assessment.
17.explain:
“So Moses’ father-in-law said to him, ‘The thing that you do is not good.”

Jethro speaks plainly. The counsel begins with an honest assessment. Moses’ way of working is “not good.”

18.brief: Jethro warns that both Moses and the people will wear themselves out, for the task is too much for him to do alone. The burden is harming both the leader and the people.
18.explain:
“Both you and these people who are with you will surely wear yourselves out.”

Both Moses and the people “will surely wear yourselves out.” The phrase pictures a leaf withering or fading. Moses would collapse from the work, and the people would be worn out by waiting.

“For this thing is too much for you; you are not able to perform it by yourself.”

The task is “too much” for one person. “You are not able to perform it by yourself.” The burden is harming both the leader and the people.

19.brief: Jethro offers counsel and says, “God will be with you,” telling Moses to stand before God for the people and bring their difficulties to Him. Moses is to keep the work of representing the people before God.
19.explain:
“Listen now to my voice; I will give you counsel, and God will be with you:”

Jethro offers “counsel” and adds “God will be with you.” He wants Moses to have God’s presence and blessing in the work.

“Stand before God for the people, so that you may bring the difficulties to God.”

Jethro’s first piece of advice is about what Moses must keep. He is to “stand before God for the people,” representing them before God and bringing the hard cases to Him. Moses is to keep the work of representing the people before God.

20.brief: Moses is also to teach them the statutes and laws and show them the way they must walk and the work they must do. Teaching God’s ways remains central to his role.
20.explain:
“And you shall teach them the statutes and the laws,”

Moses is also to “teach” the people God’s “statutes” and “laws.”

“and show them the way in which they must walk and the work they must do.”

He is to show them “the way in which they must walk,” how to live, and “the work they must do,” their duties. Teaching God’s ways remains central to his role.

21.brief: Moses is to choose able men who fear God, men of truth who hate covetousness, and set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. The new leaders must combine ability with godly character.
21.explain:
“Moreover you shall select from all the people able men,”

Moses is to choose “able men.” The word means capable, strong, of good quality.

“such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness;”

Jethro lists their character. They must “fear God,” revering Him above all. They must be “men of truth,” honest and reliable. They must hate “covetousness,” refusing bribes and dishonest gain. The new leaders must combine ability with godly character.

“and place such over them to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”

These men are to be placed over groups of different sizes, from “thousands” down to “tens.” Each level handles what it can. The apostles later followed a similar principle when they appointed men to serve tables so that they could give themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word (Acts 6:1–7). Sharing the work protects the leaders’ essential work and serves the people better.
21.notes: Deuteronomy 1:9–18 recalls this appointment, adding that the people chose wise and understanding men and Moses set them over the tribes.

22.brief: The appointed leaders will judge the people at all times, bringing great matters to Moses and judging small matters themselves, so that they bear the burden with him. Sharing the work makes it bearable for Moses.
22.explain:
“And let them judge the people at all times.”

The judges will be available “at all times.” The people will no longer wait all day.

“Then it will be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they themselves shall judge.”

The hard cases still go to Moses. The ordinary cases are decided by the judges.

“So it will be easier for you, for they will bear the burden with you.”

The judges will “bear the burden with you.” Sharing the work makes it bearable for Moses.
22.notes: Numbers 11:16–17 records a later occasion when God appointed seventy elders to share Moses’ burden, giving them His Spirit.

23.brief: Jethro says that if Moses does this “and God so commands you,” he will endure and the people will go home in peace. Jethro submits his advice to God’s direction.
23.explain:
“If you do this thing, and God so commands you,”

Jethro adds a qualification. Moses should follow the plan only if God commands it. Jethro submits his advice to God’s direction.

“then you will be able to endure, and all this people will also go to their place in peace.”

The result will be good for both. Moses will “endure,” and the people will go home “in peace,” their cases settled.

24.brief: Moses heeds his father-in-law and does all that he said. Moses humbly accepts wise counsel.
24.explain:
“So Moses heeded the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.”

Moses listens and acts. He “heeded” Jethro’s counsel. Moses humbly accepts wise counsel, even from someone outside Israel.

25.brief: Moses chooses able men from all Israel and makes them heads over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. The plan is carried out as Jethro advised.
25.explain:
“And Moses chose able men out of all Israel, and made them heads over the people:”

Moses carries out the plan. He chooses “able men” from the whole people.

“rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”

The structure matches Jethro’s advice exactly. The plan is carried out as Jethro advised.

26.brief: The leaders judge the people at all times, bringing hard cases to Moses and judging the small cases themselves. The shared leadership works as intended.
26.explain:
“So they judged the people at all times;”

The new judges serve the people “at all times.”

“the hard cases they brought to Moses, but they judged every small case themselves.”

The arrangement works. “The hard cases” go to Moses, and the judges handle “every small case.” Moses keeps the work of bringing hard matters before God, while others share the daily load. The shared leadership works as intended.

27.brief: Moses lets his father-in-law depart, and Jethro returns to his own land. The chapter closes as Israel prepares for the events at Sinai.
27.explain:
“Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went his way to his own land.”

Jethro returns “to his own land.” His visit ends in peace. The chapter closes as Israel prepares for the events at Sinai.
27.notes: Numbers 10:29–32 records Moses inviting Hobab, a relative of Jethro, to travel with Israel as a guide. Judges 1:16 mentions descendants of Moses’ father-in-law living among the people of Judah.
